name: Average-Case Modular Cryptanalysis of Subset Sum (Joux-Wegrzycki, modular arithmetic approach)
description: Average-case modular/representation cryptanalysis concerns the sparse, low-density regime of Subset Sum where one either (a) solves almost all random instances by reducing them to a lattice problem, or (b) for the hardest density-~1 regime, breaks the 2^{n/2} barrier heuristically using representation/birthday techniques with ternary coefficient sets. The focal recent result is Joux and Wegrzycki (STACS 2026), which improves the classical Lagarias-Odlyzko average-case algorithm by a modular arithmetic approach: lattice reduction is used to solve a linear system modulo a suitably large prime p, and by bounding the LLL-reduced basis vectors of the primal and dual lattices simultaneously, the admissible size of the integers drops from Omega(Gamma_LO) to Omega(sqrt(Gamma_LO)) - roughly doubling the density of solvable instances. The resulting tester is deterministic, works for all targets after a single lattice reduction, and yields polynomial-size certificates. On the density-1 frontier, ternary representations (coefficients in {-1,0,1} and {-1,0,1,2}) drive the best heuristic subset-sum attacks, e.g. Li (2025) reaches time O~(2^{0.2400n}) classically and O~(2^{0.1843n}) quantumly at density d = 1. All of this is average-case/heuristic and does not give a worst-case algorithm.
worst_case_time: Polynomial (average-case result): after a single call to a basis-reduction algorithm with parameter gamma, the algorithm builds a polynomial-time deterministic tester for the random instance, and every target T can be decided in polynomial time. Concretely, for any fixed constant c > 0, average-case instances with numbers in {1,...,Gamma_c}, log2(Gamma_c) = n^2 log log n / (c log n), are solved in n^{c+O(1)} time by the Lagarias-Odlyzko approach and in n^{c/2+O(1)} time by the Joux-Wegrzycki modular approach. No worst-case bound: for adversarial instances there is no guarantee, and the general problem remains NP-hard.
space_complexity: Polynomial in n and log(max a_i); the certificate/data structure behind the tester requires essentially a single matrix-vector multiplication (an n x n modular matrix M_p and its inverse). Lattice reduction itself uses polynomial space.
model: Classical RAM / real-number (exact integer and modular) arithmetic; lattice basis reduction with a quality parameter gamma (LLL, or textbook block reduction a la Gama-Nguyen with parameter Upsilon > 1). Randomness comes only from the uniform choice of the integers a_i; the algorithm is otherwise deterministic.
randomized_or_deterministic: The tester and its construction are deterministic; the success probability is over the random choice of the instance a_1,...,a_n and is at least 1 - 2^{-Omega(n log n)}. So it is an average-case guarantee with a deterministic algorithm and exponentially small failure probability (Las Vegas-style with a deterministic output once the matrix is built).
time_space_tradeoff_curve: Not a subset-sum time-space tradeoff; the result is polynomial time and space. The relevant parameter tradeoff is in the lattice-reduction strength: using reduction with parameter gamma -> 1 (stronger, more expensive) lets the algorithm handle a wider density range, giving running time n^{c/2+O(1)} for the density range log2(Gamma_c) = n^2 log log n / (c log n). Single point in terms of space.
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: The Joux-Wegrzycki improvement (arXiv 2024; STACS 2026) roughly doubles the admissible density: numbers of size Omega(sqrt(Gamma_LO)) instead of Omega(Gamma_LO), where log2(Gamma_LO) > n^2 log2(gamma) and Gamma_LO = (gamma_LLL)^{n^2} 2^{Theta(n log n)}. Prior density thresholds: 0.6463 (Lagarias-Odlyzko 1985) and 0.9408 (Coster et al. 1991/1992), both with an SVP oracle. On the density-1 frontier the heuristic exponents are 0.337 (HGJ 2010), 0.291 (BCJ 2011), 0.283 (BBSS 2020), and 0.2400 classical / 0.1843 quantum (Li 2025, ternary representation). Record year for the modular improvement: 2024 (preprint) / 2026 (STACS).
problem_variant: Average-case / random Subset Sum (RSSP) in the sparse low-density regime, with a unique solution with high probability; also the hard-knapsack density-~1 regime for the representation attack. Not Equal-Subset-Sum / Pigeonhole ESS, not Partition, not the general worst-case problem.
applies_to: Instances with a_i chosen uniformly at random from {1,...,ceil(sqrt(Gamma_LO))} (improved bound), for which the algorithm decides for every target T whether a {0,1} subset sums to T. The density-1 ternary-representation algorithms apply to random knapsacks of density d = 1 with exactly one expected solution, and to syndrome/information-set decoding and LWE-style problems by adaptation.
coefficient_set: The base Subset Sum has C = {0,1}. The cryptanalytic frontier uses larger signed/ternary coefficient sets: {-1,0,1} (BCJ), {-1,0,1,2} (BBSS), and the ternary tree representation of Li (2025); the extended low-density analysis of Li-Ma uses variables in {-1,0,1} with density threshold 0.488. These coefficient sets are design parameters of the representation, not the input domain.
density_regime: Sparse low-density regime. Lagarias-Odlyzko and Coster et al. cover d < 0.6463 and d < 0.9408 respectively (with an SVP oracle); Joux-Wegrzycki roughly double the admissible density by shrinking the number range to sqrt(Gamma_LO). The hard cryptographic regime is d close to 1 (hard knapsacks), which is where representation/ternary techniques apply. High density (small numbers) is handled by DP. [uncertain] the exact numeric Joux-Wegrzycki threshold expressed as a single decimal d.
solution_regime: Average-case / almost-all inherent-solution regime: for sparse instances the solution is unique with overwhelming probability, and the modular tester decides every target. The density-1 representation algorithms assume a solution exists (expected count one).
cardinality_constraint: No fixed-cardinality/Hamming-layer constraint is imposed in the modular arithmetic approach or the standard representation attacks; balanced solutions arise internally in the representation technique but the problem itself is unconstrained weight.
key_technique: Modular arithmetic approach: (1) reduce the integers modulo a prime p multiplied by a chosen scalar mu, using lattice reduction to build an n x n matrix M_p = ([mu_i a_j]_p) of centered residues with full rank and small l_1 norm (norm < p/2, i.e. no modular overflow); (2) then e is a solution iff M_p e = t_p = ([mu_i T]_p), so invert M_p and check whether the unique solution lies in {0,1}^n. The key technical step is a simultaneous length analysis of the primal and dual Lagarias-Odlyzko-style lattices (inspired by Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham small-root methods) to construct suitable mu_i when the a_i are only sqrt(Gamma_LO) large. The density-1 frontier uses the representation technique: represent one solution in many ways over signed/ternary coefficient sets, filter pseudo-solutions by modular/parity constraints, and merge lists.
core_idea: If one can find multipliers mu_i so that all centered residues [mu_i a_j]_p are small (sum of |[mu_i a_j]_p| < p/2), then the modular linear system has no wraparound and exactly replicates the integer subset-sum equation; solving the modular linear system then recovers the 0/1 solution. Bounding both primal and dual lattice vectors under LLL supplies such multipliers whenever the inputs are small enough - half the bit-length that Lagarias-Odlyzko needed - which doubles the density. Because the resulting M_p depends only on the a_i and not on T, one reduction serves all targets. On density-1 instances the analogous idea is to inflate the search space with ternary representations so each true solution has many encodings, which can then be pruned.
reduction_pipeline: Subset Sum -> linear system modulo a large prime p, built via lattice reduction (a modular Lagarias-Odlyzko/Coppersmith-style lattice) -> invert the modular matrix and test e in {0,1}^n. Equivalent to a lattice SVP/CVP reduction with a modular twist; the density-1 branch reduces Subset Sum to generalized-birthday/representation collision finding with ternary coefficient sets.
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive: the algorithm outputs the multipliers/matrix and (by inversion) the subset vector, and the tester answers for every target. The guarantee is average-case (over random a_i); there is no worst-case constructivity claim.
search_vs_decision_witness: Both. Builds a polynomial-time deterministic decision tester valid for every T (oblivious to the target), and returns an explicit solution e in {0,1}^n when one exists (and certifies non-existence when the unique modular solution is not in {0,1}^n). Constructivity is proved for the average-case input distribution.
obstacle_to_2n3: This is an average-case, polynomial-time line of work for the sparse/low-density regime; it does not produce a worst-case exponential algorithm and therefore cannot by itself reach O*(2^{n/3}) for worst-case Subset Sum. Even after doubling the density, the cryptographic hard regime at d ~ 1 lies above the provable threshold, so the worst-case/general problem remains out of reach. The density-1 representation attacks are heuristic and are still at exponent ~0.24n (far above 1/3), and their analyses rely on randomness and well-distributedness assumptions. Thus the approach advances the cryptanalytic frontier but is orthogonal to the worst-case MITM barrier.
potential_to_break_mitm: Low. It is an average-case polynomial-time enhancement of a low-density attack plus a heuristic density-1 improvement; it does not attack the worst-case general problem or improve the worst-case 2^{n/2} baseline, so it is unlikely to break the worst-case MITM barrier. Its main value is in cryptanalysis and in sharpening the density frontier.
barrier_evidence: The Lagarias-Odlyzko density guarantee stayed unimproved for nearly 40 years (1985-2024), illustrating how hard the threshold is to move. The modular improvement still only doubles the admissible density and requires random instances; adapting it to arbitrary block-reduction algorithms is technical and not fully general. Density-1 attacks are heuristic (well-distributedness assumptions) and their exponents remain well above 1/3. Independent barriers: Subset Sum is NP-hard in the worst case; SETH-based lower bounds (Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay) rule out near-linear/near-quadratic algorithms; the average-case k-SUM conjecture and planted k-SUM equivalence (Saha-Schwartzbach-Vasudevan) indicate hardness at density 1; and public-key encryption can be based on the hardness of dense/planted subset sum (Lyubashevsky-Palacio-Segev), ruling out worst-case-to-average-case collapse.
open_questions: Can the modular arithmetic approach be extended rigorously to all block-reduction algorithms (not just LLL and textbook block reduction)? Can the density threshold be pushed past the hard regime at d ~ 1, and can modular ideas be combined with ternary representation attacks? Is there a worst-case or planted-instance version of the modular tester? How far can the ternary representation exponent be lowered below 0.2400n classically / 0.1843n quantumly, and does it approach 1/3 or the MITM barrier? Can the Joux-Wegrzycki argument be applied to decoding/LWE analogues?
conditional_hypothesis: The positive results assume uniformly random input integers (average-case) and rely on LLL/block-reduction quality estimates (Hermite-factor heuristics). Hardness/limitedness statements rest on NP-hardness of Subset Sum, SETH-based lower bounds (Abboud et al.), the average-case k-SUM conjecture and planted-k-SUM equivalence, and the existence of public-key encryption from planted/dense subset sum (Lyubashevsky-Palacio-Segev). The density-1 representation analyses additionally assume well-distributed lists and a prescribed representation count.
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: Average-case only. The Joux-Wegrzycki theorem is stated for uniformly random integers in {1,...,ceil(sqrt(Gamma_LO))} and gives success probability at least 1 - 2^{-Omega(n log n)} over the instance; the algorithm is deterministic given the instance. No worst-case guarantee, and no claim for adversarially structured instances.
cryptographic_regime: Directly cryptanalytic. It sharpens the low-density attack on knapsack cryptosystems (density threshold roughly doubled relative to Lagarias-Odlyzko) and makes the attack oblivious to the target, so one lattice reduction can test many targets (relevant when an attacker sees many ciphertexts). At density ~1 the ternary-representation attacks are the state of the art for hard knapsacks and are also applied to information-set decoding and LWE-style problems.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: Complementary: this line targets sparse instances with large integers (small density), whereas dynamic programming/proximity methods target dense instances with small integers. The Joux-Wegrzycki extension explicitly studies the boundary via the density range log2(Gamma_c) = n^2 log log n / (c log n) and running time n^{c/2+O(1)}, connecting the sparse lattice regime to pseudopolynomial-style parameter tradeoffs. It does not itself use DP.

empirical_evidence: The Joux-Wegrzycki contribution is a theoretical average-case result; no benchmark implementation or experiments are reported in the paper. On the density-1 frontier, Li (2025) uses numerical optimization to obtain the exponents 0.2400n (classical) and 0.1843n (quantum), reporting asymptotic improvements over 0.283 and 0.2182 respectively; those numbers are optimization outputs rather than large-scale experiments. Concrete practical attack code is not the focus of these works. [uncertain]
implementation_artifact: No canonical public implementation of the Joux-Wegrzycki modular arithmetic tester was located; it is a theory paper (the tester is a single modular matrix plus inversion). The density-1 representation/ternary algorithms are likewise theoretical, though the underlying representation technique is implemented in cryptanalytic tools and standardized in the decoding/lattice literature. [uncertain]
verification_method: Reproduce Theorem 2 of Joux-Wegrzycki: for random a_i in {1,...,ceil(sqrt(Gamma_LO))} and a prime p = Theta((gamma_LLL)^{0.5 n^2}), run LLL on the primal and dual modular lattices, extract multipliers mu_i, verify the matrix M_p has full rank and that each row has l_1 norm < p/2, invert M_p and check that (M_p)^{-1} t is in {0,1}^n. Reproduce the density threshold by comparing Gamma_LO vs. sqrt(Gamma_LO) in end-to-end tests against a brute-force/DP reference for small n. For the ternary frontier, verify the representation counts and pseudo-solution filtering in Li (2025) / BBSS against a SAT or Meet-in-the-Middle reference.
